content: The final decision to transition from nerve tissue vaccines to modern vaccines should be based on a thorough evaluation of the safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of modern vaccines. Authorities must also assess local conditions, feasibility, and the cost implications of replacing nerve tissue vaccines. The use of cost-saving intradermal regimens for rabies preand post-exposure prophylaxis should be considered. National guidelines must be developed to provide clear instructions on the use of modern vaccines for both preand post-exposure prophylaxis. These guidelines should include indications for vaccine use, routes of administration, and guidance on the use of rabies immunoglobulin and other related products. The guidelines should be formulated by technically competent experts, drawing on recommendations from the WHO Expert Advisory Group on Rabies, other WHO advisory groups, up-to-date scientific literature, and the experiences of international and national experts. These guidelines should be disseminated to all centers providing rabies prophylaxis and should address issues such as vaccine subsidies (if applicable) and the handling of leftover vaccines. Regular updates to the guidelines are essential. Rabies centers must receive a consistent supply of safe, effective, WHO-recommended rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin from a central office. Once the decision is made to cease the production and use of nerve tissue vaccines, procurement of modern vaccines should begin immediately to prevent any gaps in treatment availability. Coordination with regulatory bodies is crucial for the registration of new rabies biologics and for post-marketing surveillance of new rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin. A network of specialized bite centers should be established, staffed with personnel trained in administering preand post-exposure prophylaxis and managing adverse reactions. These centers must maintain adequate quantities of rabies biologics. A referral system should be implemented to maximize the benefits of the intradermal regimen and minimize vaccine wastage. A quality assurance system with standardized protocols should be instituted across all centers. Provincial and municipal governments should play a role in establishing new centers, ensuring a sustainable supply of rabies vaccines, immunoglobulin, and other supplies, and guaranteeing the reporting, investigation of human rabies cases, and monitoring of the rabies program. The intradermal route of rabies vaccine administration is safe, immunogenic, and more cost-effective than the standard intramuscular route. It is particularly recommended in settings with limited vaccine and financial resources. Rabies vaccines labeled for intramuscular use can be safely administered intradermally, even if this constitutes off-label use. Intradermal administration is suitable for immunocompromised individuals or those receiving immunosuppressive therapies such as chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, or long-term corticosteroids. Reconstituted vaccines must be refrigerated and used within six hours, as they do not contain preservatives. Before administering rabies vaccines intradermally, all staff must be adequately trained in the intradermal injection technique. The wound should be thoroughly washed, and, if applicable, the appropriate dose of rabies immunoglobulin should be administered. A 1.0 mL syringe (insulin or tuberculin syringe) with a short, fine hypodermic needle should be used. Fixed-needle syringes are preferred to reduce void volume and save costs. The intradermal schedule should be selected based on the specific case. For intradermal administration, the vaccine should be aseptically reconstituted immediately before use with the diluent provided by the manufacturer. The correct volume of vaccine should be drawn into the syringe, ensuring sterile precautions and the removal of air bubbles. The injection site should be disinfected with an antiseptic, and the skin should be stretched before inserting the needle into the dermis at an angle almost parallel to the skin surface. A raised papule resembling orange peel should appear immediately, measuring 6–8 mm in diameter. If the injection is too deep, it should be repeated. Reconstituted vaccine can be used for multiple patients, but a sterile syringe and needle must be used for each patient. The vaccine must be stored at 2–8°C and used within six hours. Post-exposure prophylaxis should be administered based on the category of exposure. For minor scratches or abrasions without bleeding (Category II), the vaccine should be administered immediately, and treatment can be stopped if the animal remains healthy during a 10-day observation period or is proven negative for rabies by reliable laboratory testing. For severe exposures (Category III), both rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin should be administered as soon as possible. Rabies immunoglobulin can be given up to seven days after the first vaccine dose. Treatment can be stopped if the animal remains healthy during the observation period or is confirmed negative for rabies. Rabies vaccination certificates should be carefully maintained by vaccinated individuals as part of their personal health records. Blank certificates should be supplied by vaccine manufacturers. Post-exposure vaccination regimens include options such as a one-week, two-site intradermal schedule (days 0, 3, and 7), a two-week, one-site intramuscular schedule (days 0, 3, 7, and between days 14–28), or a three-week intramuscular schedule (days 0, 7, and 21). Individuals who have received at least two sessions of rabies vaccination (preor post-exposure) are considered previously immunized. Verbal autopsy questionnaires should be used to investigate suspected rabies cases, collecting detailed information about the patient’s exposure history, symptoms, and treatment. Contact investigations should identify individuals who had contact with the suspected rabies case or the animal involved, and risk assessments should be conducted to rule out potential exposure. Human rabies cases should be classified as suspected, probable, or confirmed based on clinical and laboratory findings.
